entries.title: Vikings lose wide receiver Justin Jefferson in 23-16 win over Buccaneers
entries.summary: <p>TAMPA, Fla. — Myles Price returned a punt 86 yards for a score, Kyler Murray threw a 41-yard TD pass to Jordan Addison and the Minnesota Vikings beat the Tampa Bay Buccaneers 23-16 on Sunday.</p><p>It was a costly game for both teams.</p><p>Baker Mayfield hurt his thumb on a desperation pass late in the fourth quarter. He was screaming in pain on the ground before walking off and was replaced by rookie Jalon Daniels in the final minute.</p><p>Two-time All-Pro wide receiver Justin Jefferson didn't return for Minnesota after injuring his right ankle in the first quarter.</p><p>The Vikings are 3-0 for the second time in three years. The Buccaneers are 0-3 for the first time since 2014, when they finished 2-14 and got the No. 1 overall draft pick, taking Jameis Winston.</p><p>Murray was 15 of 29 for 168 yards with one TD pass and one interception in his first full game with the Vikings. He sustained a concussion in the first quarter of the season opener and Carson Wentz led Minnesota to consecutive wins.</p><p>Mayfield hasn't played like a $55 million-a-year quarterback since the Buccaneers gave him a $165 million extension before the season. He was 17 of 34 for 217 yards with one TD and one interception, taking six sacks.</p><p>Tampa Bay's woeful offense couldn't do much against coordinator Brian Flores' defense.</p><p>Mayfield had an 85-yard touchdown pass to Chris Godwin Jr. on third-and-30 negated by a holding penalty on Luke Goedeke in the third quarter.</p><p>That summed up the offense's struggles.</p><p>Mayfield's 14-yard scramble on second-and-9 later was negated by a holding penalty on Payne Durham. But the Bucs got a first down on third-and-29 when Joshua Metellus hit Emeka Egbuka helmet-to-helmet. Again, the offense had to settle for a field goal. Chase McLauglin's 54-yarder cut it to 17-16.</p><p>Will Reichard's 56-yard field goal extended Minnesota's lead to 20-16 with 3:10 remaining. He added a 43-yarder to cap the scoring.</p><p>Murray connected with Addison on a deep throw on third-and-8 to give the Vikings a 17-10 lead in the second quarter. Addison beat Jacob Parrish in one-on-one coverage, making a smooth adjustment on the ball.</p><p>After A'Shawn Robinson intercepted Murray's pass to set up a first down at the Vikings 22 in the third quarter, the Bucs went nowhere. Bucky Irving ran 3 yards and then dropped a pass. Mayfield got sacked on third down and McLaughlin's 38-yarder cut it to 17-13.</p><p>The Buccaneers fell behind 10-0 after just one possession. Following a three-and-out, Price darted up the middle, cut to the right and sprinted down the sideline for his first career touchdown.</p><p>Mayfield fired a 40-yard TD pass down the seam to rookie Ted Hurst III to cut it to 10-7.</p><p>The Buccaneers had a first down at Minnesota's 7 after Mayfield and Cade Otton connected on a 37-yard pass. But consecutive holding penalties on Cody Mauch and Graham Barton derailed the drive and McLaughlin kicked a 28-yard field goal to tie it.</p><h3>Brotherly love</h3><p>Buccaneers left guard Ben Bredeson played against his younger brother, Vikings rookie fullback Max Bredeson. Their older brother, Jack, is the director of player information for the New York Mets. All three went to Michigan.</p><h3>Injuries</h3><h3></h3><p><b>Vikings:</b> Jefferson injured his right ankle when a defender fell on it. He walked to the locker room after watching a couple series. ... P Brett Thorson (hamstring) was inactive. ... CB Charles Demmings left with a hamstring injury.</p><p><b>Buccaneers:</b> Edge rusher Rueben Bain Jr. (groin) and LB Josiah Trotter (shoulder) were inactive. ... WR Jalen McMillan left in the first quarter with a knee injury and didn't return.</p><h3>Up next</h3><h3></h3><p><b>Vikings:</b> Host Miami next Sunday.</p><p><b>Buccaneers:</b> Host Green Bay next Sunday.<br></p>

entries.title: Lyons' EJ Kuhlman is on a roll
entries.summary: <p>Playing high school football and baseball keeps Lyons senior EJ Kuhlman pretty busy.</p><p>But what does he do in his downtime?</p><p>“I love playing pickleball with my friends,” Kuhlman told the Sun-Times. “I think that’s actually got me on my toes.”</p><p>There’s no doubt the 5-9, 177-pound Kuhlman’s footwork is elite.</p><p>He’s in his second season as the lead running back for the Lions (5-1, 2-1 West Suburban Silver), who have clinched their sixth consecutive IHSA playoff berth.</p><p>Last year against York in the regular season, Kuhlman ran 43 times for a program-record 246 yards. Some other records could be in play this season, but he’s not interested in talking about them.</p><p>“My main goal is just winning conference first,” he said. “I don’t really care about the stuff that comes with it.</p><p>“I mean, it’s awesome to get those records at the end of the season, see what you’ve achieved. But you can’t really put all that credit on yourself . . . because you know a lot of that comes from coaches and O-linemen.”</p><p>He had 1,104 rushing yards and 15 touchdowns last fall and has scored at least one touchdown in every game this season with multiple 100-yard rushing games.</p><p>It’s a culmination of everything Kuhlman has been working toward.</p><p>“I always played flag football growing up, but I didn’t start tackle until seventh grade,” he said. “I was with the LFC [Lyons Football Club] program, and it was with a lot of my same buddies I play with now.”</p><p>Like most kids, Kuhlman tried a variety of sports growing up: soccer, basketball, tennis and wrestling in addition to the ones he’s still doing.</p><p>“You kind of play whatever your parents put you in,” he said. “Sports has always been part of my life, and it’s a big part of me and who I am.”</p><p>Until last year, Kuhlman didn’t really favor one sport over the other.</p><p>“Honestly, I was always split between baseball and football,” he said. “But junior year, I think I took football a lot more serious. I think I started to appreciate it a lot more. The amount of effort that goes into football is kind of what took me to love football more than baseball.</p><p>“But I still love both sports, very close to equal. But football is just a little different for me.”</p><p>That meant an extra level of preparation for his final high school season, focusing primarily on getting faster.</p><p>“Speed’s the biggest factor with a running back,” he said. “So you drop a couple of pounds to gain that extra point-one or point-two on that 40 [yard dash time].</p><p>“But I think this year, my goal is just to try not to get down — always break that first guy.”</p><p>The season of experience has paid off in other ways.</p><p>“What [is] different this year is kind of [being] comfortable,” Kuhlman said. “And I feel like [it’s been] to slow the game down and just realize that you kind of control it.”</p>

entries.title: Man charged with shooting of 1-year-old girl in Chicago Lawn home
entries.summary: <p>A man was charged with the shooting Saturday of a 1-year-old girl in a Chicago Lawn home on the South Side. </p><p>Davaris Washington, 38, was charged with reckless discharge of a firearm, unlawful use of a machine gun, reckless conduct causing great bodily harm and possession of a firearm by a repeat offender, Chicago police said. </p><p>Washington was arrested around 12:15 a.m. Saturday in the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/09/26/girl-found-shot-inside-chicago-lawn-home" target="_blank" >6400 block of South Mozart Street</a> where the girl was found shot minutes earlier, police said. </p><p>She was taken to Comer Children's Hospital in critical condition, officials said. </p><p>Washington is expected to appear in court Monday. </p>

entries.title: Cubs! White Sox! Playoffs! Keep chanting those words and maybe, just maybe, it'll last more than a few days
entries.summary: <p>Are you ready for both the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" target="_blank" >Cubs</a> and the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" target="_blank" >White Sox</a> in the playoffs?</p><p>For God’s sake, somebody has to be.</p><p>Are the Cubs themselves ready? It’s a bit hard to believe in that after they spent the final days of the regular season losing back-to-back critical games at Wrigley Field to the going-nowhere Marlins, then <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/09/25/cubs-red-sox-doubleheader-tampa-playoff-rotation-mlb-postseason-clay-holmes-david-peterson" target="_blank" >gagging on both ends of a doubleheader</a> in Boston, to rob themselves of a sweet chance at home-field advantage in a wild-card series against the Padres that starts Tuesday.</p><p>Instead, off to San Diego they went after a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/09/27/cubs-alex-bregman-face-home-runs-red-sox-mlb-postseason-playoffs-series-padres-world-series" target="_blank" >meaningless 6-2 win Sunday</a> against the Red Sox in St. Petersburg, Florida — look, don’t ask — a 2,000-plus-mile flight during which a travel-weary Cubs team was left to wrestle with some uncomfortable questions.</p><p>“Can we hit anymore?”</p><p>“If we have an ace, where might he be hiding?”</p><p>“Bullpen? What bullpen?”</p><p>And then there are the Sox, who are as experienced at playing postseason baseball as the average bob of seals is at filming TikTok dances. They’ll be in Houston, also starting Tuesday, against a .500 Astros team that owns the distinction of being the worst division champ, by record, in major league history. Despite that, the Sox are the betting underdogs, presumably having something to do with the fact they lost approximately 8.4 billion games from 2023 to 2025.</p><p>Unlike the 89-win Cubs, though, this year’s 84-win Sox finished strong, winning back-to-back-to-back series against the Tigers, Royals and Rockies. Alas, it wasn’t enough to out-sprint the Guardians to the finish line for a division title simply because the Guardians woke up one mid-September morning having inhabited the bodies of the 1927 Yankees. Maybe this is Cleveland’s year to end the majors’ longest current World Series championship drought? It would be a shocker, but it’s possible.</p><p>The Sox, on the other hand? Bless their hearts, they’re just babies.</p><p>Still, you might as well take everything you’ve read thus far in this column, wad it up and drop-kick it onto the nearest trash pile, because this is no time for negativity. It’s only the fourth time both Chicago teams have made it to the postseason, which makes this a mighty big occasion. And can’t we all agree our city was home to baseball’s best two stories this season — the out-of-nowhere emergence of the Sox and the all-out explosion of Cubs MVP-to-be Pete Crow-Armstrong?</p><p>What a thing these Sox have pulled off. Back on Opening Day in Milwaukee, I watched them lose 14-2 to the Brewers and thought: <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/03/26/white-sox-win-total-2026-mlb-opening-day-chris-getz-will-venable-brewers" target="_blank" >Here we go again</a>. But even though general manager Chris Getz and manager Will Venable wouldn’t talk then about what improvement would look like in terms of a number of victories, some around the team were openly confident. TV analyst Steve Stone, a self-described psychic, told me the Sox were going to win “well above” outside expectations. Radio analyst Darrin Jackson thought 80 wins was possible. And second baseman Chase Meidroth had the temerity to use the P-word — “playoffs” — freely.</p><p>“We’re going to compete our asses off,” Meidroth said then.</p><p>I didn’t buy any of it.</p><p>Yeah, well, go suck an egg, Greenberg.</p><p>Despite Getz going in on starting pitcher Luis Castillo at the trade deadline — a failed move — the Sox’ season has been a success no matter what happens against the Astros or, if the Sox actually survive that series, against the Guardians after that.</p><p>Not so for the Cubs, who won’t have anything compelling to hang their hats on if they don’t advance further in Craig Counsell’s third year as manager and Jed Hoyer’s sixth year as president of baseball operations than they did in 2025.</p><p>Last season’s Cubs were good enough to beat the Padres in the wild-card round at Wrigley, but they couldn’t measure up to their prime tormentors, the Brewers, in the divisional round after that. This year, the richest team in the division finished so far behind the small-market Brewers — 14 games — it might take all the gumption the Cubs have just to show their faces in Milwaukee should they get past the Padres again.</p><p>The Cubs were 10-13 in September, but they’ve been less than impressive for a lot longer than that. Over the last four and a half months, they’ve been essentially a .500 team.</p><p>It won’t be as painful in San Diego as the last time the Cubs played playoff baseball there — yep, 1984 — but I don’t think they’ll make it to Milwaukee. An underwhelming season is nearing the end.</p><p>I’ve got the Astros in three, too.</p><p>Either that or a Red Line World Series, right?</p><p>Here we go.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/sports-media/2026/09/27/chicago-cubs-white-sox-mlb-postseason-playoffs-padres-astros-nbc-nbcsn-peacock-streaming-prime-video-xfinity-fubo-youtubetv" >Cubs, White Sox fans take one on chin from wild-card TV</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/sports/2026/09/24/what-do-i-need-to-know-chicago-cubs-white-sox-both-mlb-playoffs-postseason" target="_blank" >What do I need to know about the Chicago Cubs and White Sox both being in the MLB playoffs?</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>
entries.author: Steve Greenberg

entries.title: White Sox wrap up magical season with victory and still hope to turn page in postseason
entries.summary: <p>In many respects, the 162nd game of the 2026 <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" target="_blank" >White Sox</a> season played out like those of recent years.</p><p>Their 4-2 victory against the Rockies had zero stakes for either side, many reserves filled out the box score and the announced home attendance for the season clocked in at less than 2 million fans (1,986,419).</p><p>The difference was that the nearly 30,000 fans on hand Sunday pushed the full-season figure to the Sox’ highest total since 2022, the only season in the last 15 they’ve eclipsed 2 million fans. Rather than sticking around just in case some lesser-known members of the roster might toss free T-shirts into the stands, fans remained to roar in support of a Sox team headed to Houston for the franchise’s first postseason action in five years.</p><p>It’s easy to imagine a darker context in which an injured pitcher carries one of the highest Q scores on the roster. But the cheers that crested as Mike Vasil raised a fist to the crowd — his other arm around third baseman Miguel Vargas, the Sox’ best player — offered a warm feeling about what this team has become.</p><p>‘‘The way the fans have come out and supported these guys and given them energy, to watch that back-and-forth grow throughout the season has been amazing,’’ manager Will Venable said.</p><p>The Sox won only 84 games, but they did so in front of fans that reasoned 75 victories was an aspirational goal and repaid the unexpected success in enthusiasm.</p><p>Could the Sox have won more? They certainly thought so and rued a slide in early September that cost them the American League Central title.</p><p>They also had 11 walk-off victories and often strung together pitching plans that would have made MacGyver nervous. Plus, no team that has tied itself spiritually to the papacy the way these Sox have can consider themselves starved of blessings.</p><p>‘‘I don’t think anyone saw the kind of success that we had, and I think it was really fun to be a part of,’’ said left-hander Anthony Kay, who earned the victory Sunday.</p><p>The Sox also are boarding their flight to Houston hoping for a reset. They went 34-33 after the All-Star break, allowing the Guardians to catch and overtake them for the division title and dealing them a sting they still were shaking off Sunday.</p><p>‘‘We were pissed,’’ shortstop Colson Montgomery said. ‘‘We had a lot of vocal people. Everyone was just like, ‘We’ve got important games coming up.’ ’’</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" data-embed> <iframe width="113" height="200" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/M409Kh4iA7Q?feature=oembed" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen title="The White Sox' Colson Montgomery on moving on from the division race and focusing on the playoffs"></iframe> </div> </div></div><p>Perhaps no one better represents the Sox’ quest for an October rebirth than Montgomery. He socked 31 home runs and was dominant during the 18-10 May that launched the Sox onto the national scene, but he is craving a clean slate after a poor second half. He also set MLB’s single-season strikeout record, about which he admitted, ‘‘You don’t want your name to be a part of.’’</p><p>The Sox dropped five of seven games this season to the Astros across two series that featured some of their lowest moments, strategic moves that Venable openly second-guessed.</p><p>‘‘We were scuffling as a whole,’’ veteran outfielder/designated hitter Randal Grichuk said, referring to the Sox losing three of four games to the Astros in Houston from Aug. 31 to Sept. 3. ‘‘We match up well with them.’’</p><p>Are the Sox capable of a deep playoff run? The uncertainty of their rotation suggests otherwise, but that would assume anyone not aboard their flight to Houston understands how and why they have been good all season.</p><p>‘‘Our focus is just on us,’’ designated hitter Andrew Benintendi said. ‘‘Everybody in here knows what we can do.’’</p><p>Would knocking off an 81-81 Astros team be a monumental accomplishment? No. But it’s doable.</p><p>It would be the Sox’ first victory in a postseason series in 21 years. And it would be fun, which is the quality that brought nearly 2 million fans to Rate Field this season.</p>
entries.author: James Fegan

entries.title: Alex Bregman homers twice in season-finale win, Cubs head to playoffs aiming to ‘make some noise in October’
entries.summary: <p>ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. — A week after a fouled-off baseball did <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/09/23/cubs-alex-bregman-face-injury-return-matt-shaw-bunt-daniel-palencia-stats" >significant damage to Alex Bregman’s face</a>, Bregman returned the favor, doling out punishment to the baseballs.</p><p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" >Cubs</a>’ third baseman launched a pair of home runs as part of a four-hit day in a 6-2 win over the Red Sox in the regular-season finale Sunday, showing the type of impact he can make as the team eyes a deep playoff run.</p><p>“I did want to feel good before the playoffs,” Bregman said. “I wanted my swing to feel like it did right before I got hit. I felt good mechanically today.”</p><p>Bregman, the $175 million free-agent signee who figures to be a key factor in how far this team can go in the postseason, continues to marvel his fellow Cubs with what he’s doing, by merely taking the field so quickly after what happened.</p><p>“I’m not surprised that he’s performing when he’s back on the field. I’m surprised that he’s back on the field,” manager Craig Counsell said. “Him being back on the field is what we should all appreciate and admire.</p><p>“This is not normal that a player is back on the field right now after what he’s been through. You still see what he looks like, frankly, and that tells you what he’s still going through. That’s what I’m surprised by.</p><p>“But his performance, I don’t think it surprises you.”</p><p>Indeed, this is the sort of thing the Cubs long expected from the uber-accomplished Bregman, even back when he was mired in such a deep slump that he was getting booed at Wrigley Field.</p><p>His manager and teammates assumed he would finish the season with the sort of numbers he’s put up throughout his career, and wouldn’t you know it, that’s what happened.</p><p>Thanks to a huge second half, Bregman wrapped the campaign with 28 home runs — the third-highest total of his career — and a right-where-it’s-supposed-to-be .819 OPS.</p><p>“The first four months of the season, I don’t know what that was. I’m embarrassed to have put that on tape,” Bregman said. “But the last two months of the season, that’s who I am as a player. I’m proud to know that, no matter how big of a hole I dug myself, I found my way back out of it and [finished with an OPS] over .800.</p><p>“I learned a lot this year, and I feel like I got better as a pro.”</p><p>After the Cubs scored just nine runs over their five previous games, they wrapped their regular season with a half dozen on Sunday, finally escaping the chilly, windy conditions of Wrigley Field and Fenway Park in <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/09/25/cubs-red-sox-game-moved-boston-weather-fenway-park-tampa-bay-florida-tropicana-field" >a game relocated to Florida</a>.</p><p>While it might not wipe away all fan concerns over what’s possible in the postseason, it was a good day for the bats — they banged out 13 hits — ahead of <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/09/26/cubs-playoff-matchup-padres-nl-wild-card-standings-mlb-postseason-san-diego-phillies-diamondbacks" >a trip to San Diego</a> for a best-of-three playoff series against the Padres.</p><p>There are <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/09/26/cubs-regular-season-finale-playoffs-mlb-postseason-nl-wild-card-standings-offense-lineup-pitching-rotation" >a lot of questions following the Cubs</a> as they head to the West Coast and the lights get their brightest. But their long-held championship-level goals are still in front of them.</p><p>And the belief hasn’t left the clubhouse.</p><p>“When you show up to spring training, that’s what you work the whole offseason for, to start this and be able to play meaningful games in October. That’s exactly what we’ve done,” lefty reliever Ryan Rolison said. “It hasn’t been perfect this year. We’ve been through a lot of adversity, guys stepping up in spots. Now we’re here, and we’re going to make some noise here in October.”</p><p>“When we put games together,” righty reliever Ryan Zeferjahn said, “I don’t know who can beat us.”</p><p>For Bregman, the two-time World Series champ who’s done <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/09/14/cubs-alex-bregman-career-playoff-games-postseason-world-series-braves-nl-wild-card-standings-mlb-playoff-matchups-carson-kelly-sprint-speed" >more than almost any other hitter in postseason history</a>, he sees in these Cubs the right ingredients for the sort of success he’s had previously in his career.</p><p>“A togetherness. An attention to detail,” he said. “Guys that know what they do well and know what they need to do to prepare.</p><p>“When it comes to the playoffs, it comes down to executing. You’re playing against the best teams in the world. If you do that, you’re in a good spot.”</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/sports-media/2026/09/27/chicago-cubs-white-sox-mlb-postseason-playoffs-padres-astros-nbc-nbcsn-peacock-streaming-prime-video-xfinity-fubo-youtubetv" >Cubs, White Sox fans take one on chin from wild-card TV</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: Cubs, White Sox fans take one on chin from wild-card TV
entries.summary: <p>Chicago baseball fans got the shaft when MLB released the schedule Sunday for the Cubs’ and White Sox’ wild-card series. NBC has the rights to the first-round matchups, but Games 1 and 2 for the Cubs and Sox were relegated to the network’s streaming service, Peacock, and NBC Sports Network, to which you might not have access.</p><p>The ballyhooed Red Sox-Yankees rivalry — which the nation always is subjected to more than necessary — naturally was given the prime-time spot on over-the-air NBC for the first two games of its series. The network also will air the first two games of the Phillies-Braves series in the afternoon. The best-of-three wild-card series are scheduled to run Tuesday to Thursday.</p><p>To watch Games 1 and 2 of Cubs-Padres and White Sox-Astros, fans must watch on Peacock, which costs $12.99 per month, or NBCSN, which is available on Comcast’s Xfinity system and streamers Fubo and YouTube TV. Though Xfinity and YouTube TV are two of the largest pay-TV providers in the country, NBCSN is missing from services such as DirecTV and Astound/RCN.</p><p>For the Sox, Games 1 and 2 are scheduled for 4 p.m. For the Cubs, they’re set for 9. The start time for a possible Game 3 of either series will depend on how many series are still going.</p><p>These aren’t the first major postseason games stuck on a streamer. The NFL put the Packers-Bears playoff game in January on Prime Video, but it was available locally over the air. The NBA streamed 28 first- and second-round playoff games exclusively on Peacock (seven, which also aired on NBCSN) and Prime Video (21) last season.</p><p>But they are the first MLB postseason games to air on a streaming service. It was part of NBC’s deal that gave it “Sunday Night Baseball,” which had aired on ESPN for 36 seasons, and the wild-card round. The rest of the American League playoffs will air on TBS; Fox and FS1 have the rest of the National League playoffs. The World Series will air on Fox.</p><p>Here’s some good news: NBC will continue its use of local analysts on national broadcasts. Steve Stone will be on the call for the Sox’ series, and Jim Deshaies will be in the booth for the Cubs’ series.</p>

entries.title: Wrong-way driver slams into car, killing woman on South DuSable Lake Shore Drive
entries.summary: <p>A motorist driving the wrong way slammed into another car, killing a woman inside it late Sunday on the South Side. </p><p>Around 11:20 p.m., a black SUV drove in the wrong direction and struck a white sedan head-on in the 4000 block of DuSable Lake Shore Drive, Chicago police said. </p><p>The 35-year-old woman, who was in the sedan, was taken to Northwestern Memorial Hospital where she died, police said. </p><p>No other injuries were reported. </p><p>The Major Accidents Investigation Unit is investigating.</p>
entries.author: Sun-Times Wire

entries.title: Family spat leaves man fatally shot in Greater Grand Crossing
entries.summary: <p>A family argument turned violent when a man fatally shot his sister's boyfriend late Sunday in Greater Grand Crossing, according to a police report. </p><p>Police responded to a call of a person shot about 10:40 p.m. in the 500 block of East 76th Street, and found Mark Hurn, 54, with gunshot wounds to his chest, abdomen and legs, according to the report.</p><p>Hurn was taken to the University of Chicago Medical Center where he was pronounced dead at 11:22 p.m., according to police and the Cook County medical examiner's office. </p><p>A witness told officers a family argument erupted about the alleged shooter and the care of his mother. During the quarrel the alleged shooter became hostile toward the 54-year-old and asked him to "step outside,'' according to the report. </p><p>Relatives still inside the house then heard three gunshots ring out, found the 54-year-old, who was the boyfriend of the alleged shooter's sister, and the alleged shooter running away, the report said. </p><p>Area 2 detectives were investigating. </p>
entries.author: Sun-Times Wire

entries.title: Dear Abby: Recuperating elder does not need a houseguest
entries.summary: <p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> My father is in his mid-80s. He has been to the hospital several times in the last month because of age-related medical conditions. A family member is vacationing here and wants to stay at dad's house for a week instead of a hotel or bed-and-breakfast. Dad told me he's not feeling up to it, but he doesn't know how to tell them without upsetting them.</p><p>I passed this message to the family member, and they agreed. A week later, they announced that they were going to come anyway and would be there on a certain date. How do I explain that this is too much for him? Having guests stay at your house is a lot of work and can create a lot of stress. — <i>GET A ROOM</i></p><p><b>DEAR GET A ROOM:</b> It was presumptuous of this family member to invite themselves in the first place. It is beyond the pale to insist on coming after being told they would be a burden to your ailing father. Your dad's health and well-being must come first, so stop worrying about upsetting this person. Suggest a nice place for them to stay when they come to town, and be as blunt as necessary when you tell them they are not staying with your dad.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> I am a widow in my early 60s. I have had a best friend for 50 years. For the most part, we get along great and rarely have disagreements, partly because I don't like conflict or confrontation. I usually let it go if I do not agree with something she has said. Recently, she made a comment I found disturbing and personally derogatory. I immediately called her out on it, and we had a strongly worded argument. We haven't spoken since. I can't decide whether to give her a call to try to smooth things out. If I do, I worry she may continue to belittle me. What do you think? — <i>GROOVY MAMA</i></p><p><b>DEAR GROOVY:</b> Do you miss your friend? It seems like you would like to give her another chance. I say give her a call. You don't have to mention the insult. Just invite her to a meal or other activity you both enjoy, and try to have a good time. If she doesn't manage her tongue better, calmly ask her to stop hurting your feelings. Be clear that if she keeps it up, there will be no more chances.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> When I expect a visitor, it seems like I'm always rushing to be ready on time and, at the last minute, I need to use the bathroom. If it's someone I don't know well, or maybe someone I have never met, I debate whether I should dash to the bathroom and leave a note on the door saying, "I'll be there in a few minutes," or wait for the person to come in and immediately excuse myself. I worry that if my guest is late, I may be uncomfortable. What would be the best way to handle this? — <i>NATURE CALLING</i></p><p><b>DEAR NATURE CALLING:</b> When nature calls, one cannot ignore it. If you would be comfortable inviting the person in and telling them you'll be with them "in a minute," I think it would be more hospitable than leaving a note on your door.</p><p><i>Dear Abby is written by Abigail Van Buren. For nearly four decades, Jeanne Phillips penned this column, which was founded in 1956 by her mother, Pauline Phillips. Contact Dear Abby at www.DearAbby.com or P.O. Box 270135, Kansas City, MO 64127.</i></p>

entries.title: Monday Night Football: What to watch for in Bears-Eagles when each team has the ball
entries.summary: <p>Breaking down what to expect Monday night when <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >the Bears</a> host the Eagles:</p><p><b>WHEN THE BEARS HAVE THE BALL</b></p><p>When Bears general manager <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2024/09/02/like-it-was-meant-to-be-bears-gm-ryan-poles-rebuild-comes-together-faster-than-he-or-anyone-imagined" >Ryan Poles</a> set out to rebuild the Bears’ defensive line in the 2025 offseason, he pointed to the Eagles’ “waves of pass rushers” as something he wanted to emulate. No matter who plays quarterback for the Bears, time could be short in the pocket.</p><p>The Eagles actually are off to a slow start up front and had just three sacks and got pressure on only 22.6% of pass plays over their first two games. They also allowed 254 yards rushing.</p><p>Nonetheless, with players like defensive tackle Jalen Carter and linebacker Zack Baun and a world-class defensive coordinator Vic Fangio, that’s likely to click into place sooner than later. The Eagles will put the Bears’ offensive line through its toughest test of the season to date.</p><p>That won’t be a problem for some. Right tackle Darnell Wright, right guard Jonah Jackson and future Hall of Fame left guard Joe Thuney can hold their own against anyone.</p><p>There are concerns, though, about left tackle Braxton Jones and center Garrett Bradbury. While coach Ben Johnson gave both of them a vote of confidence publicly over the past week, Jones was in a rotation with Theo Benedet against the Vikings and Bradbury committed four penalties.</p><p>The Bears’ big-picture plans are for Ozzy Trapilo to step in at left tackle and Logan Jones to take over at center, but Trapilo likely is still at least a week away as the team plays it cautiously with him and Jones is in line to be a starter next season.</p><p><b>WHEN THE EAGLES HAVE THE BALL</b></p><p>The Philadelphia fan base never seems happy enough with quarterback Jalen Hurts, but he rarely misses a game, has a triple-digit passer rating over the last three seasons and has won six playoff games, including a Super Bowl. Most franchises build statues for guys like that.</p><p>Even in a relatively poor game last week against the Titans, Hurts managed 264 yards passing and 16 rushing as the Eagles won 24-20 on his touchdown pass to wide receiver Darius Cooper with nine seconds left.</p><p>Hurts was fifth at his position with 421 yards rushing last season, including two games of 60 or more, and the Bears typically have had trouble with dual-threat quarterbacks as they slow down the pass rush even more and often force the defense to use a linebacker as a spy.</p><p>That said, one of his worst games last season was against the Bears. While Hurts totaled 261 yards combined passing and rushing and threw two touchdown passes, he managed an 84.2 passer rating, threw an interception and lost a fumble on a Tush Push as the Bears won 24-15. They did that despite cornerbacks Jaylon Johnson and Kyler Gordon playing at far less than 100%.</p><p>The Bears are off to a solid start up front and will need more of that against a top-five offensive line. While the defense had only five sacks over the first two games, it had a 37.3 pressure rate, which ranked third in the league.</p>

entries.title: Woman alleges in new lawsuit she was sexually abused as a teen in 1990s at the Willow Creek megachurch
entries.summary: <p>Willow Creek Community Church in South Barrington, one of the country’s largest and best-known evangelical congregations, doesn’t just aim to fix souls, it also fixes vehicles through what’s called the “C.A.R.S. Ministry.”</p><p>Vehicle owners in financial need can qualify for low-cost repairs through the program, which stands for Christian Automotive Repair Service and involves mechanics working in an auto shop on church property.</p><p>Donated vehicles are also accepted, fixed up and sold or given away, with eligibility for a freebie “based on but not limited to income level, intended use of vehicle and involvement at Willow,” according to a church website.</p><p>A man named Robert John Condon was working there in the 1990s when a girl, 15 or so at the time, was hired by the church to handle clerical tasks for the C.A.R.S. Ministry.</p><p>A resident of the northwest suburbs, she and her family attended Willow Creek, at the time run by the charismatic founding pastor Bill Hybels.</p><p>What started out as an exciting job — and somewhat challenging, as she was told she would have to learn to drive stick-shift vehicles — quickly turned dark, as Condon began allegedly grooming her over a number of months and eventually sexually abused her.</p><p>That’s according to a recent lawsuit the woman filed in Cook County court against Willow Creek, in what’s the latest in several troubling misconduct allegations involving the church over the last decade.</p><p>In 2017 and 2018, Willow Creek agreed to pay more than $3 million to resolve other lawsuits alleging another man, church volunteer Robert Sobczak Jr., molested special needs children at the church, according to court records, interviews and published accounts.</p><p>Church leaders were accused of ignoring red flags that could have prevented at least some of the sexual abuse.</p><p>Also in 2018, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2018/4/10/18409415/willow-creek-founding-pastor-bill-hybels-steps-down-amid-misconduct-allegations" target="_blank" >Hybels left his position amid accusations</a> of sexual misconduct against women at the church, though he denied wrongdoing. He couldn’t be reached for comment. Nor could Condon.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-2d0000" name="image-2d0000"></a> My mom said, ‘If you don’t leave, I’m going to call the cops.’ He wouldn’t tell her what was going on and eventually left.</p><p>“I didn’t give them a lot of information about what had happened ... with the mind frame of how we grew up and how we were taught, it’s shameful to share something.”</p><p>But she said she told her parents enough they knew the basics.</p><h3>Read the new lawsuit below</h3><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" data-embed> <iframe src="https://docs.google.com/viewer?embedded=true&url=https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/e1/07/3f48b6d14d47bb3953ea4cbfecf9/janedoelawsuitwillowcreek.pdf"></iframe> </div> </div></div><p>The lawsuit states between “approximately 1997 and 1998, Condon sexually harassed, sexually touched, sexually abused, and/or sexually assaulted Plaintiff, including touching her in a sexual manner while at Willow Creek Church” without “any consent.”</p><p>The accuser said her parents had “gone to someone else they knew in the church, he was an elder, and they told him what they thought had happened. I really think my parents trusted that, they were so indoctrinated into that.”</p><p>She believes Condon told someone, too — Willow Creek leaders, though it’s unclear whether Hybels was among them. She said she knows this because during one service, she heard her name mentioned by the pastor, who handed the microphone to Condon, who was also in attendance.</p><p>“They gave him a platform ... he stood up, and he never denied what he did, he admitted what he’d done,” she said. “It fell to the excuse that he’s a sex addict, and he was repenting and he was very sorry that he did this to me, and they announced during that time that he was going to be put on leave to get some therapy, treatment, whatever, and he’d be on that leave for a year.” It's unclear if a video of that service exists.</p><p>“They let him have his job back” well before then, she said. “I was never spoken to, my parents were never spoken to.”</p><p>“I was basically never acknowledged.”</p><div child was abused by a youth leader, but nothing was done and another child was then molested.</p><p>The Willow Creek suit explains how its accuser's accusations surfaced: “Prior to August 2024, the repression of these memories, the psychological effects that caused her to repress, block out, and not be aware of them, until such time as they returned to her in August 2024, was also the direct result of the nature of the sexual trauma committed by Condon when she was a child.”</p><p>As an adult, she said she came forward to the church, seeking an acknowledgment of what she believes was entries.title: Cook County Board President Toni Preckwinkle accepted campaign money from union amid talks with her agencies
entries.summary: <p>It’s widely known that Mayor Brandon Johnson’s campaign has been heavily funded by labor unions that he holds influence over, a legal but ethically questionable practice.</p><p>One of Johnson’s political mentors, Cook County Board President Toni Preckwinkle, has been doing the same — accepting millions of dollars in campaign contributions from labor groups that her administration negotiates collective bargaining agreements with, records show.</p><p>But a Chicago Sun-Times review found Preckwinkle at times has taken this a step further — accepting contributions while union negotiations are pending with county agencies she helps oversee.</p><p>Recent examples involve Teamsters Local 700, which represents about 10,000 public sector employees. Among them: more than 200 maintenance and other workers with the Cook County Forest Preserve District who went on strike in August and reached an agreement earlier this month that ended the walk out.</p><p>Contract talks between Local 700 and the Forest Preserve District began in May 2025, according to the agency, whose oversight board is composed of Cook County Board members and headed by Preckwinkle.</p><p>Local 700’s political action committee gave $10,000 to the Preckwinkle for President campaign fund in a contribution dated March 17, 2026, according to the Illinois State Board of Elections.</p><p>That was the date of the primary election that saw Preckwinkle face a well-funded opponent in Ald. Brendan Reilly (42nd), though she ended up <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/03/17/cook-county-president-democratic-illinois-primary-results" >winning handily </a>and is now moving to the Nov. 3 general election in which there’s a Libertarian opponent, Michael Murphy, but no Republican.</p><p>The Local 700 contribution appears to be the largest given by the group to the Preckwinkle fund in a decade. It’s unclear whether the money was solicited by the Preckwinkle campaign.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a entries.title: Illinois passed the nation’s first climate migration law. The effort has languished since
entries.summary: <p>When Gov. JB Pritzker signed the Climate Displacement Act last fall, Illinois became the only state in the country to enact legislation aimed at anticipating the ways in which climate-driven migration could transform life for its existing residents and those who may come after climate disasters elsewhere.</p><p>The law established a task force to investigate how domestic and international climate migration patterns could test Illinois’ infrastructure, resources and residents. And it required the newly formed team to publish two reports over the next two years outlining the state’s ability to address climate migration through at least 2050.</p><p>If Illinois succeeds, it could become a blueprint for how states make room for those displaced by climate catastrophes.</p><p>But only a year later, state officials have largely neglected their plans. Lawmakers have pushed back reporting deadlines and are yet to convene the task force, even though the first report is due in December.</p><p>Climate disasters <a class="Link" href="https://www.internal-displacement.org/focus-areas/Displacement-disasters-and-climate-change/" target="_blank" ><u>force millions of people</u></a> to leave their homes every year, growing the population of those commonly referred to as climate migrants who are on the move without specific legal protections. In the aftermath of floods, fires, and droughts, they face the challenge of finding a new place to rebuild their lives.</p><p>The hotter the planet grows, the higher the number of climate migrants is expected to climb. At the low end, experts <a class="Link" href="https://www.worldbank.org/en/news/press-release/2021/09/13/climate-change-could-force-216-million-people-to-migrate-within-their-own-countries-by-2050" target="_blank" ><u>predict at least 44 million people</u></a> across the globe will be displaced within their own countries by 2050. That’s the equivalent of rehoming the entire population of Argentina. Very few places are planning for this possibility — making Illinois’ novel effort even more attention-grabbing.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Migrants often trek through treacherous conditions, such as the infamous Darien Gap, to reach safer locations in the aftermath of climate disasters that displaced them from their homes.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>John Moore/Getty Images</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Pritzker, the state's top lawmakers and the heads of several state agencies were supposed to appoint members to the board no later than 90 days after the law went into effect. Until last week, only a single <a class="Link" href="https://govappointments.illinois.gov/boardsandcommissions/details/?id=a8c2be07-6e7c-f011-b4cb-001dd8095d99" target="_blank" ><u>appointment had been made</u></a> to the 17-seat task force.</p><p>WBEZ and Grist reached out to the state officials responsible for appointing the board, including Pritzker, four members of the Illinois General Assembly and the heads of seven state agencies.</p><p>“Governor Pritzker remains committed to fighting climate change and preparing Illinois for its impacts, including climate-related migration,” Jose Correa, a spokesperson for the governor, said in a statement to WBEZ and Grist. “This work is important, and the administration will continue working with lawmakers, state agencies, and stakeholders to establish a timeline and move the task force forward.”</p><p>The Governor’s office did not provide an estimate for when a timeline would be available.</p><p>Illinois Senate President Don Harmon responded to WBEZ and Grist by saying he would file paperwork to appoint state Senator Graciela Guzman, who represents Chicago, to the task force after being contacted for comment.</p><p>“We haven't received a clear answer,” said Guzman, when asked about the delays plaguing the Climate Displacement Act, the law she helped pass last fall. “This has been two years in the making … I’m honored to serve on the Climate Displacement Task Force and ready to get to work.”</p><p>The first report, due at the end of the year, requires the task force to compile the latest data and scientific findings to determine the scale of climate migration expected within the United States and neighboring countries in the coming decades. The second report, due at the end of 2027, is supposed to assess how state agencies and existing programs will need to evolve in response to disaster-induced displacement.</p><p>Guzman, born to Salvadoran refugees in Los Angeles, introduced the bill in February 2025, just a month after 14 wildfires tore through southern California, scorching tens of thousands of homes and buildings in the second- and third-most destructive fires in the state’s history.</p><p>“My family, like many families there, were having some really real conversations: If these wildfires were to encroach upon the valley where they lived, where would they go?” she said.</p><p>They could come to Illinois.</p><p>The temperate Midwestern state is an agricultural powerhouse, adjacent to 20% of the world’s unfrozen freshwater, relatively safe from hurricanes and wildfires and is far enough inland that sea level rise is not an immediate risk.</p><p>Given these favorable conditions, Chicago, the state of Illinois and the Midwest have sometimes been billed as “<a class="Link" href="https://www.chicagobusiness.com/crains-forum-climate-migrants/climate-change-extreme-weather-migration-great-lakes/" target="_blank" ><u>climate havens</u></a>,” a term for destinations marketed as insulated from extreme weather. But scientists and policy experts have pushed back on <a class="Link" href="https://www.chicagotribune.com/2026/08/10/editorial-climate-migration-could-be-a-big-boost-for-chicago/" target="_blank" ><u>these claims</u></a> for years, <a class="Link" href="https://investigatemidwest.org/2023/07/03/midwest-states-often-billed-as-climate-havens-suffer-summer-of-smoke-drought-heat/" target="_blank" ><u>countering that no such place exists</u></a>. They say the nature of climate change is global, and rising temperatures will have cascading knock-on effects on all life on the planet — including the Midwest, where climate change has been leaving its mark.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-810000" name="image-810000"></a> <picture data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>People survey the damage after a tornado ravaged a residential neighborhood in Aroma Park, Ill., in March 2026.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Tyler Pasciak LaRiviere/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>This past year, Chicago residents experienced significant and widespread flooding when its massive tunnel and reservoir system <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/environment/2026/07/06/chicago-deep-tunnel-historic-flooding-tarp-reservoir-weather-climate-change" target="_blank" ><u>very nearly hit capacity</u></a>. A record-breaking number of <a class="Link" href="https://grist.org/extreme-weather/even-meteorologists-are-baffled-by-the-midwestern-tornado-season/" target="_blank" ><u>tornadoes</u></a>, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/weather/2026/09/01/september-october-chicago-heat-wave-is-this-normal" target="_blank" ><u>extreme heat</u></a> and wildfire smoke that <a class="Link" href="https://grist.org/equity/after-a-civil-rights-complaint-chicago-built-the-nations-largest-air-monitoring-network/" target="_blank" ><u>significantly worsened</u></a> air quality levels for nearly a full week made the past summer unlike any recent memory.</p><p>“It's all that anybody I'm around is talking about — just the incredible weather events that we have had in our state,” Guzman said. “It’s really laying bare why this kind of planning is important.”</p><p>Climate haven or not, she said the law is an opportunity for the state to understand its resources and plan for the potential influx of new residents — which could mean building affordable housing or creating new job programs. But before any of that can happen, the state needs a roadmap.</p><p>Illinois is the only state that has given itself an explicit mandate to prepare for population shifts due to climate change. However, other states have begun enacting or at least considering climate-related relocation. Maine has incorporated climate migration into broader statewide <a class="Link" href="https://mainemorningstar.com/2023/10/20/environment-immigrant-groups-say-state-needs-to-prepare-for-likely-climate-migration/" target="_blank" ><u>resilience planning</u></a>. And lawmakers in California, Hawaii and New Jersey have introduced bills to begin planning for the protection of coastal communities vulnerable to rising sea levels and buy out some of the most at-risk properties.</p><p>Earlier this year, Alaska lawmakers passed a law pledging to help the low-lying, coastal communities of Kipnuk and Kwigillingok <a class="Link" href="https://www.npr.org/2025/12/15/nx-s1-5596136/alaska-storm-native-climate-change" target="_blank" ><u>relocate in the devastating aftermath of Typhoon Halong</u></a>.</p><p>In the Midwest, Cincinnati <a class="Link" href="https://www.cincinnati-oh.gov/oes/news/climate-migration-readiness-plan-published/" target="_blank" ><u>city officials circulated a blueprint</u></a> to accommodate upwards of 500,000 new residents by 2050. The plan doesn’t market the city as “climate-proof.” Instead, it outlines ways to improve the quality of life for residents by increasing the availability of affordable housing and investing in public transportation — similar to Illinois’ proposal.</p><p>Illinois still has a long road ahead, according to Byran Jones, a geographer and professor at Baruch College in New York City, who has worked on landmark climate displacement and relocation reports.</p><p>“It's a daunting task, and the state of Illinois needs to recognize that,” he said.</p><p>Part of the issue is that the term “climate migrant” is relatively new, and it has no universally agreed upon definition. Climate refugees also have no legal recognition under international law. Most modern-day protections for refugees are based on the 1951 Refugee Convention, which <a class="Link" href="https://www.unhcr.org/media/1951-refugee-convention-and-1967-protocol-relating-status-refugees" target="_blank" ><u>restricted the definition</u></a> to someone “persecuted for reasons of race, religion, nationality, membership of a particular social group, or political opinion.”</p><p>Modeling climate change and migration independently is also difficult enough without trying to account for the two together. Migration alone is a complicated phenomenon driven by factors ranging from economic prospects to family ties, gender and poverty, making it difficult to project even before adding the pressure of climate change.</p><p>But Jones said that Illinois officials can build on existing research by identifying what makes the state special — such as its vast agricultural sector and major metropolitan area — and modeling how it could influence migration patterns. The work, he said, will be time-consuming, but climate change is already affecting migration patterns, and the best way to limit disruptions is to plan.</p><p>“It would be of tremendous service and certainly help to get the conversation started where there's been limited conversation in this country, to this point,” Jones said.</p><p><i>This coverage is made possible through a partnership between WBEZ and</i><a class="Link" href="http://grist.org/" target="_blank" ><i> Grist</i></a><i>, a nonprofit environmental media organization.</i></p>

>Refugee with genetic disorder faces loss of health care</a></h3><p></p><h5>Reporting by <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydjilriy-l-k/" target="_blank" >Elvia Malagón</a></h5><p><b>Omar's story</b>: Omar, 19, has Duchenne muscular dystrophy, a condition that leaves him unable to breathe, eat or walk on his own. His parents, Mahmoud and Asmaa, are his caretakers. The three are Syrian refugees whose application for permanent residency in the U.S. is pending. Omar's parents say they worry about what will happen to his health come Thursday, when they, along with an estimated 9,300 other immigrants in Illinois, are expected to lose Medicaid coverage.</p><p><b>Key context</b>: As part of H.R.1, known as President Donald Trump's "One Big Beautiful Bill," refugees will no longer be eligible to receive Medicaid, a state-federal program that provides health coverage to low-income households and people living with disabilities. It's part of a larger overhaul the <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydjilriy-l-u/" target="_blank" >Trump administration is making to Medicaid</a>, including new work requirements.</p><p><b>Bottom line</b>: The new eligibility changes will also result in a loss of coverage for immigrants seeking asylum and those who entered the country through humanitarian parole, such as those fleeing the war in Ukraine, according to the state. Other immigrants, like naturalized citizens, permanent residents, children and pregnant individuals, will remain eligible.</p><p><a class="Link" It's gonna be a fun October here in Chicago." — <i>Ryan Esquivel</i></p><p>"That we hate Green Bay." — <i>Donnette Strukl</i></p><hr><p>Thanks for reading the Sun-Times Morning Edition!<br>Got a story you think we missed? <a class="Link" href="mailto:newsletters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >Email us here.</a></p><hr><p><b>Written and curated by</b>: Matt Moore<br><b>Editor</b>: Michael Lansu<br><b>Copy edited by</b>: Satchel Price</p>

entries.title: Man shot, critically wounded during West Pullman home invasion
entries.summary: <p>Police are looking for two gunmen who burst into a West Pullman home and shot a man, critically injuring him early Monday during a home invasion in West Pullman.</p><p>The 20-year-old man was inside his home in the 11800 block of South Princeton Avenue around 2:40 a.m. when two gunmen entered and opened fire, Chicago police said. </p><p>The man was struck multiple times in the body and was taken to the Advocate Christ Medical Center in Oak Lawn where he was in critical condition, police said. </p><p>The gunmen fled the scene on foot, officials said. </p><p>Area 2 detectives were investigating. </p>

entries.title: Review: Klaus Mäkelä brings forth the innately raw, edgy intensity of Shostakovich’s Symphony No. 4
entries.summary: <p>While critical opinion might be mixed on Klaus Mäkelä, who will become the full-fledged artistic director of the Chicago Symphony Orchestra next fall, the Chicago audience has completely embraced the 30-year-old Finnish conductor with his fresh-faced flair.</p><p>That became very clear Thursday evening, when the CSO’s music director designate returned for his first-ever three-week run with the ensemble and received an ardent round of cheers before one note had even sounded.</p><p>After more than a decade of steadfast artistic leadership from <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2023/6/9/23753881/riccardo-muti-legacy-chicago-symphony-orchestra" target="_blank" >Riccardo Muti</a>, one of the incontrovertibly great conductors of his generation, the CSO took a radically new direction in 2024 and put its faith in a young talent it hopes will become the next great conductor.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-4e0000" name="module-4e0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>Chicago Symphony Orchestra, Klaus Mäkelä, conductor</h3><br><b>When:</b> Oct. 1-4 (“Mahler 9”), Oct. 8-9 and Oct. 10 (“Petrushka” and “Belshazzar’s Feast”), at Symphony Ball<br><b>Where:</b> Orchestra Hall, 220 S. Michigan Ave.<br><b>Tickets:</b> Oct. 1-4, $59+<br><b>Info</b>: <a class="Link" href="https://chicagosymphony.org/" target="_blank" >chicagosymphony.org</a></div> </div><p>Like the orchestras in San Francisco and New York, who have also recently appointed music directors, the CSO is resetting its direction and trying to appeal to new audiences.</p><p>Reinforcing this notion of a renewal was the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/classical-music/2026/09/24/chicago-symphony-orchestra-cso-rebrand-nonprofit-logo-music-classical" target="_blank" >CSO’s announcement</a> earlier Thursday of a rebranding, complete with a streamlined new red logo and modified names like relabeling the ensemble’s building complex as Chicago Symphony Center.</p><p>But more important than names and looks is the music itself, and Mäkelä and the CSO stumbled a bit out of the gate Thursday during Jean Sibelius’ compact Symphony No. 7 in C major, Op. 105, with characteristic Nordic reserve and an episodic structure. While there were some striking individual moments in this performance, it just never cohered into a compelling whole.</p><p>But any deficiencies in that performance were quickly forgotten once the evening’s main attraction got underway — Shostakovich’s towering Symphony No. 4 in C minor, Op. 43, which ran about an hour and required an augmented orchestra including nine French horns and eight percussionists.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-c60000" name="image-c60000"></a> class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Principal Timpani David Herbert and Assistant Principal Timpani and Percussion Vadim Karpinos perform Shostakovich’s Symphony No. 4, led by CSO Music Director Designate Klaus Mäkelä.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Todd Rosenberg</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Unlike the in-your-face musical evocation of artillery discharges and goose-stepping soldiers in some of the composer’s symphonies, this symphony is suffused with palpable pain — both Shostakovich’s own and that of his country living under Stalin’s brutal, repressive regime.</p><p>He finished the score in May 1936 just a few months after he had been denounced in a Pravda article infamously titled “Muddle Instead of Music.” He wisely filed away the symphony, which could have gotten him banned or worse, and it was not premiered until a less tense time in 1961.</p><p>The mood can be angry, manic, discordant or mournful, sometimes in quick succession or almost all at once. There is a sense of organized chaos, with one musical phrase interrupting, cutting off or crashing into another. The woodwinds and brass exchanging musical slap shots. The clarinets voicing a quirky, unsettling ditty. The strings delivering strange, punctuating pizzicato bursts.</p><p>Unusual sounds abound, like the unexpected appearance of castanets and weird, ghostly passages from the usually celestial celeste near the haunting conclusion of the third movement, and others where it wasn’t clear how exactly they are being produced.</p><p>To pull off this symphony requires a performance that is raw, edgy and intense, and that is exactly what Mäkelä and the CSO delivered. He arguably could have leaned even more into those qualities, but this was an emotionally devastating (in the best sense of the word) take by any measure.</p><p>And back to that notion of “organized chaos,” the maestro negotiated the hairpin turns and sudden lurches with pinpoint command and never let the throughline become lost or the emotional intensity droop. Yet, at the same time, he brought forth the music’s innately unsettled, off-kilter and sometimes almost out-of-control feel.</p><p>This work allows absolutely every instrument in the orchestra to have moments in the spotlight, and these musicians made the most of them. Examples include principal trombonist Timothy Higgins’ fine playing in the third movement and a searching first-movement solo from the CSO’s always-wonderful English hornist Scott Hostetler.</p><div 7.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Todd Rosenberg</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>We’re starting to get a better understanding of the kinds of repertoire that appeals to Mäkelä, especially his enthusiasm for less frequently heard music by famous composers, like the choice of Symphony No. 4. It is hardly unknown but had not been played by the CSO for nearly two decades.</p><p>An even clearer example of this penchant will come Oct. 8-10 when Mäkelä and the ensemble present rare performances of William Walton’s 1931 oratorio, “Belshazzar’s Feast,” which nearly fell out of the repertory in the 1970s.</p><p>Mäkelä was clearly the musicians’ choice as their new music director, and it’s exciting to watch the rapport between them deepen, to see him mature and develop before our eyes and to find out how this musical marriage ultimately plays out.</p>

entries.title: Where to go apple picking near Chicago, Indiana and Wisconsin
entries.summary: <p>While the changing color of the leaves is always a trustworthy sign of autumn’s arrival, apples cropping up at orchards across the Midwest are another.</p><p>Corn mazes, cider doughnuts, petting zoos and plenty of u-pick apples (as well as sunflowers, raspberries and pumpkins in some cases) await at farms in Illinois, Indiana and Wisconsin within driving distance of Chicago where families can pluck fruit fresh from the tree and enjoy plenty of other seasonal activities.</p><p>“We feel like this is a place for families to create lasting memories,” said Annette Jenkins, representative at All Seasons Orchard in suburban Woodstock. “It’s also an opportunity to relax, spend time together and slow down. I love going out in the orchard and hearing the laughter and seeing parents playing games with their kids and one another.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" Vazquez/Sun-Times</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Anthony Vazquez/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Fans of Dolly Parton won’t want to miss this year’s corn maze. In the works for the last three years and in partnership with Parton’s Imagination Library, the 6-acre maze pays tribute to the late singer and is carved in her likeness. A portion of the proceeds will be donated to local chapters to help with Imagination Library.</p><p> “We are honoring her in a different way than we anticipated,” said Jenkins, referencing Parton’s recent sudden passing last month. “She represents the same values we have as far as agriculture and family.”</p><p>Over at Jonamac Orchard in Malta, the farm fun extends into the evenings on Saturdays with homemade hard cider and apple wine along with live music, food trucks and a flashlight corn maze.</p><p>“It's a nice, laid-back way to enjoy the orchard at night,” said Gabri Zmich, guest relations manager, adding that kids are welcome. </p><p>While this past early spring’s bad weather affected many orchards, “The good news is we are past that now, and we have so many great varieties,” said Jenny Fahey of Peck & Bushel in Colgate, Wisconsin. She’s particularly excited about the orchard’s organic CrimsonCrisp. “It’s tart and sweet and has such an explosive flavor.”</p><p>Nothing quite compares to a freshly picked apple, according to Brittany Richey, co-owner of Honey Hill Orchard in Waterman. “Take a bite of one of the just-picked apples and you quickly realize it tastes so much better than one from the store,” she said, adding, “The experience teaches kids how to gather their own food.” </p><p>Here are nine orchards all within driving distance of Chicago, perfect for a day trip.</p><h3><a class="Link" href="https://allseasonsorchard.com/" target="_blank" ><b>All Seasons Orchard</b></a></h3><p><i>14510 IL Route 176, Woodstock; 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. weekdays, 10 a.m. to 6 p.m.  Saturdays and Sundays. Through Nov. 1.</i></p><p>Honeycrisp fans will want to add All Seasons to the must-visit list. This farm boasts one of the largest orchards of the popular sweet-tart variety, which ripens in September. “We are well known for our Honeycrisps and they go fast,” said Annette Jenkins, representative for the orchard. “When they’re gone, they’re gone.”</p><p> But if you’re looking for another variety, an up-to-date list of what’s available can be found on All Seasons’ online apple availability calendar. In addition to Honeycrisp, EverCrisp — a Fuji-Honeycrisp hybrid available later in the season — and Zestar are other apple varieties to look out for, added Jenkins. </p><p><b>Family fun:</b> The “fun farm” includes a ropes course, petting zoo, pig races, pony rides, u-pick pumpkin patches, a bee observation station and a Dolly Parton-themed corn maze. Be sure to say hello to Moe the Scottish Highlander, who has been at the farm dating back to the original owners and has plenty of fans. Goats, alpacas, and zebu and Watusi cows also call All Seasons Orchard home.</p><p><b> On the menu:</b> Food offerings range from pulled pork sandwiches and loaded fries to burgers and cheese curds. Sweet treats include ice cream sundaes, apple cider doughnuts, cotton candy and kettle corn. Pair it all with freshly squeezed lemonade.</p><p><b>Pro tip: </b>To avoid the weekend rush, swing by during the week before 11:30 a.m. except on Tuesdays when they’re closed. </div><p>Honey Hill Orchard offers a “laid-back and quiet country atmosphere,” co-owner Brittany Richey said. “What makes us special is we’ve been able to stay small and keep it simple. This is a place for folks to relax and experience Mother Nature.” On the weekends, wagon rides to the orchard and pumpkin patch, weather permitting, add to the farm-life experience. With nearly 40 different varieties of apples, Honey Hill’s most popular offerings include Gala and Honeycrisp.</p><p><b>Animal encounters:</b> Petting zoo animals include a donkey, goats, sheep, chickens and rabbits. Towering over the other animals, Eddy the Belgian Draft horse is hard to miss, said Richey. You can buy food to offer the animals, but Richey notes that they appreciate apples and doughnuts, too. The children’s play area features a straw maze to explore.</p><p><b> On the menu:</b> All of the orchard favorites like apple cider doughnuts, cider slushies, homemade caramel apples, freshly pressed apple cider and apple pies are available. The apple cider doughnut sundae is a must-try, according to Richey. On the weekends, food trucks, offering a diverse lineup of fare ranging from tacos and barbecue to ribeye sandwiches, pull up from 11 a.m. to 3 p.m.</p><p><b>Pro tip:</b> U-pick pumpkins and raspberries and the orchard’s own honey are also available. The farm’s sunflower patch makes a great backdrop for a family photo. Take note: Sunflower season came early this year but pre-cut sunflowers are for sale. </p><p><b>Cost: </b>$13 per person for a quarter-peck bag and includes a weekend-only orchard wagon ride.</p><hr><p></p><h3><a class="Link" href="https://www.kuipersfamilyfarm.com/" target="_blank" ><b>Kuipers Family Farm</b></a></h3><p><i>1N145 Watson Road, Maple Park; hours vary throughout the season until Nov. 25. Check the website for days and hours. (For weekly updated apple varieties, call 815-827-5200.)</i></p><p>In 1998, when Wade and Kim Kuipers opened their 71-acre farm, its pumpkin patch was the star. Now 230 acres, it’s a seasonal farm boasting 45 apple varieties. This season, don’t delay your apple-picking outing. “Due to the warm spring weather we experienced, our apples are ripening several weeks earlier than usual this year and we encourage guests who want to experience u-pick apple picking to visit early in the season,” said Joe Kuipers, general manager of the farm and son of Wade and Kim. “It’s shaping up to be a beautiful crop, but the picking window may be shorter than in a typical year.”</p><p><b>Pumpkins:</b> The Pumpkin FunFarm is open through Nov. 1 for visitors to pick their gourds and enjoy outdoor activities, including corn and bale mazes, jumping pillow, mountain slide, farm animals, hay wagon rides, apple blaster, giant corn box, live music, food trucks, adult beverages and more.</p><p><b>Let them entertain you:</b> On the weekends, Kuipers hosts live music and bands. There are also pig races (with an apple cider doughnut as the grand prize), adult beverages from the Farmyard bar and a variety of food trucks on the Pumpkin FunFarm. </p><p><b>Cost: </b>Customers can purchase tickets online for $14.99 per person for weekends and holidays; select weekday tickets may be purchased at the gate for $11.99 each. Orchard</b></a></h3><p><i>19412 Shabbona Road, Malta; daily 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. Through mid-October. The farm is open until Nov. 25.</i></p><p>With a pumpkin patch, corn maze, petting zoo, wine and hard cider, this family-owned and operated orchard offers something for every member of the family to enjoy. The four-generational family operation has been in business since 1984, when Gerald and Mary Lynn McArtor purchased a farm from the Johnson family, changing the name to “Jonamac” in honor of the families. </p><p>Jonamac prides itself on using sustainable practices, from encouraging natural predators and pollinators to practicing crop rotation and utilizing cover crops. </p><p>“We are very lucky that we weathered all the frosts this spring, so we have about 80% of our crop available,” said Gabri Zmich, guest relations manager.</p><p><b>Action-packed weekends:</b> Pony rides are on offer, but for the adventurous, guests can ride a camel on weekends. There are also duck races, apple cannons, a corn maze and more. Apple tokens are required for some activities. Private party firepits can be rented, providing a landing spot for groups and proximity to the live music on the weekends. Visit the Cider House for homemade hard cider and apple wine, available to take home too.</p><p><b>Crop news:</b> Leaning into sustainability, Jonamac doesn’t include Honeycrisps in its pick-your-own activity, although they are available in the store. “We know that’s everyone’s favorite, but we’re trying to protect those trees,” said Zmich. She recommends Pazazz apples instead. “They’re beautiful to look at and delicious too. We think they're even better than Honeycrisps.”</p><p><b>Pro tip:</b> Sign up for Apple Alerts on Jonamac’s website for updates on when your favorites are available. To beat the crowds, visit in the morning or late afternoon, Zmich recommended.</p><p><b>Cost: </b>Visiting the store and bakery is free, but buying a general admission ticket is required on weekends and holidays to visit the activity area, which includes access to the cider house, orchard, flower field and pumpkin patch. Buy online for a $2 discount. A bag also must be purchased to pick apples; pricing for u-pick starts at $16 for a half-peck. Up to four people per picking bag.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-800000" >Apple Holler</a></h3><p>5006 South Sylvania Ave., Sturtevant, Wisconsin; orchard and farm park open 8:30 a.m. to 4 p.m. Monday through Thursday; 8:30 a.m. to 5 p.m. Friday through Sunday. Through early November, weather permitting.</p><p>Located about 90 minutes north of Chicago, Apple Holler offers not only 40-plus varieties of the fruit, but also plums, nectarines, pears and peaches for picking during the season. The family farm began in 1987 when Dave and Vicki Flannery bought the then-abandoned orchard. The couple began planting trees and flipped the milking barn into a bakery. Nearly 40 years later, the Flannerys continue to run the farm.</p><p><b>Animal encounters:</b> This summer the farm welcomed 15 baby goats, said manager Elyse Muchka. On the weekend, the farm offers pony rides along with rubber duck races. There’s a chicken coop too.</p><p><b>Adults only:</b> On the weekends, Apple Holler has a beer garden that features hard ciders and craft beers on tap as well as Bloody Marys and mimosas along with live music.</p><p><b>On the menu:</b> A new weekend drip-and-doughnuts trailer features specialty lattes like pumpkin spice and apple cider, handcrafted cookies and doughnuts, all made on-site. Food stands offer pizza, hot dogs, hamburgers, brats and more. The orchard additionally offers a small farm store. During the week, head to Red Barn Restaurant for heartier fare like steak and eggs, prime rib French dip and chicken pot pie.</p><p><b>Autumn activities:</b> Kids can explore an “enchanted forest” where there are a number of characters in the trees. The family fun park features a corn maze, giant slides and pedal karts. New this year is a bubble hut. Learn about the apple varieties and the farm’s growing process while taking the tractor-drawn train ride to the orchard. “The education part is fun here, too,” said Muchka.</p><p><b>Cost:</b> U-pick pricing starts at $26 per person for a quarter-peck bag and includes a tractor-drawn train tour of the orchard family farm and enchanted forest and all-day access to the Kids Korral Play Area.</p><div County Line Road, Hobart, Indiana; Big Barn open daily 8 a.m. to 6 p.m.; attractions open from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. Through Nov. 1.</p><p>Located in Hobart, Indiana, about an hour southwest from Chicago is County Line Orchard. Known for its annual corn maze, the orchard went viral in 2024 after revealing a maze in the shape of WNBA star Caitlin Clark. This year’s maze, “Fifty Nifty Apples States,” features a map of the U.S. and is a celebration of apples across the country, what makes them special and the stories behind. County Line features a selection of nearly 30 apple varieties alongside pumpkins and sunflowers for picking. Kids of all ages will appreciate the Moo Choo, a unique Farmall Cub tractor and cart combo that travels around the farm. This year, apples available for picking are limited due to spring frosts and summer storms, but fresh apples are available in the Big Barn.</p><p><b>Animal encounters:</b> The kids farm features chickens, goats, pigs and a donkey. Check out County Line’s bee yurts, which help make the apple orchard possible via pollination.</p><p><b>On the menu:</b> In the Brat Barn, try the seasonally inspired Harvest Brat (beer brat, sauerkraut, apple butter and brown mustard). For those who like it hot, there’s also a spicy brat with Flaming Hot Cheetos and candied jalapenos. The Kitchen Restaurant offers homemade Orchard Bowls, with options like meatballs and fried chicken paired with mashed potatoes, gravy and corn.</p><p><b>Cost:</b> Admission without apple picking begins at $5 with free admission for children 2 and under. Pick or pack apples are $2 a pound.</p><hr><p></p><h3><a class="Link" href="https://www.peckandbushel.com/" target="_blank" >Peck & Bushel Organic Fruit Company</a></h3><p>5454 County Road Q, Colgate, Wisconsin; open 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. Fridays, Saturdays and Sundays. Through the end of October.</p><p>This family farm northwest of Milwaukee was runner-up in USA Today’s vote for the best apple orchard in the nation. “We’re the largest certified organic apple orchard for pick your own in the upper Midwest,” said Jenny Fahey. “We like to think of ourselves as more of a specialty place. It’s not just apple picking but really being in nature.” The farm boasts over 50,000 dwarf apple and fruit trees over 80 acres, which are grown on a trellis system similar to a vineyard making for the fruit easier to grow.</p><p><b>On the menu:</b> At its on-site bakery, choose from specialties like apple cider slushies (made from Peck & Bushel’s own organic cider), apple sticky bread, cream puff apple cider doughnuts and gourmet caramel apples. The Cidery, Peck & Bushel’s wedding venue, features a selection of sandwiches, including apple fritter ham and cheese, turkey apple brie and Italian grinders. Wraps, salads and a small kids menu round out the menu, along with adult beverages. Enjoy it all outside, where “there’s a great porch that looks out onto the orchard,” said Fahey.</p><p><b>What’s in store:</b> In addition to pre-picked apples, baked goods, jams, jellies and freshly pressed organic cider, the store includes home goods, gifts and kid-centric items. During the first few weekends in October, be on the lookout for organic cranberries from a local purveyor along with cranberry-focus baked goods and beverages.</p><p><b>Pro tip:</b> No reservations are needed at the orchard, but Fahey says there’s no need to worry about having to wait to get in. She recommends waiting out the early crowds and arriving an hour later at 11 a.m.</p><p><b>Cost:</b> U-pick pricing starts at $12 for a quarter-peck bag.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center>
